title: The palace in flames (Genesis Rabbah 39:1)
hookLine: Abraham sees a burning palace and asks if it has no owner; the owner looks out
tomorrow: Jacob lay down on stones. he woke up with one. how?

lines: A PALACE, LIT UP. OR BURNING.
cards: Night, on a long road. A traveler comes over a rise and sees a great building, a palace, lit up from inside. Or burning.
He stops. Nobody runs out with buckets. Nobody runs in.
And he asks out loud, to no one at all: is it possible this palace has no one in charge of it?

teach.h: A PALACE, AND NO ONE AROUND.
teach.b: Genesis Rabbah tells this parable about Abraham, just before God says to him, "Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house."

teach.h: I AM THE MASTER OF THIS PALACE.
teach.b: In the parable, the master of the palace looks out at the traveler and says: I am the master of this palace. So with Abraham, the midrash says. He kept asking: is it possible the world has no one guiding it?

And the Holy One looked out at him and said: I am the Master of the world. Here's the twist. The Hebrew phrase, birah doleket, can be heard as a palace full of light or a palace in flames, and readers take it both ways.
Lit up: Abraham sees the world's order and beauty and asks who built it.
In flames: Abraham sees a world full of cruelty and fire and asks how its owner can let it burn.
Either way, Abraham doesn't pretend the palace is fine. He asks out loud.
And the owner doesn't scold him for asking. He looks out, and answers: I'm here, it's mine. Then, right after, the call: get thee out.
In this story the one who asks who's in charge is the one who gets sent.

how: Genesis Rabbah 39:1 is studied with the Torah portion Lech Lecha, where God calls Abraham to leave home; the parable is a favorite in classes on faith and questioning.

Genesis explains how Abraham came to know God

games.q: the news is full of fires, real and otherwise. a friend says: if anyone were in charge, this wouldn't happen. what does Abraham's palace give you?
o: ask it out loud, like Abraham; in the midrash the owner looks out.
stop asking; questions like that just show a lack of faith.
decide no one's in charge; a burning palace proves it's empty.
games.why: Abraham's question isn't punished. the master looks out and answers, and right after, Abraham is sent.

practice: Listen for one sound around you that means someone is looking after something: a fridge humming, a furnace, traffic lights, a neighbor's footsteps. Stay with that one sound for the sit.
Let it carry the traveler's question: who keeps this going?
